summary: A mobile application for monitoring an astronaut's health status, adapted for the iPads used during space missions. The app is cross-platform—compatible with both iOS and Android—making it ideal for use during space missions as well as at astronaut training centers on Earth. The central element of the tablet interface is an interactive 3D model of the astronaut (a digital twin). It functions as a visual health map: healthy organs and systems are highlighted in green, areas of concern in yellow, and critical issues in red. Tapping on a specific body part (such as the heart or leg muscles) opens a side panel displaying dynamic charts that track changes in health metrics over time.
details:
The primary function of the application is to monitor and detect health issues in astronauts. To facilitate user interaction within an environment of limited resources, a Small Language Model (SLM) has been integrated, serving as an interactive medical reference guide. Astronauts can ask questions using natural language—for example, "What should I do if I experience pain in my right knee during a centrifuge test?" The SLM utilizes Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) based on medical protocols to provide instant, step-by-step instructions.

Moving beyond a dry output like "87% probability of an issue," the system employs the concept of explainable AI. The SLM generates clear, actionable text: "Your sleep schedule and elevated heart rate indicate stress. I recommend performing a breathing exercise and adjusting your cabin lighting to 4800K."

Additionally, the SLM can act as a conversational partner to monitor the crew's mental health and mood by analyzing text or voice input.

A gamification and routine management module ensures comprehensive engagement; astronauts can view their daily "missions"—such as progress on centrifuge training, vitamin intake, or reaction-time tests. Alongside this, an AI assistant (SLM) interface—presented as a chat—allows users to seek explanations for anomalies in their data or obtain step-by-step guidance on first aid and the operation of specialized equipment. The system operates entirely locally, simulating conditions where there is no connection to Earth. The frontend is built using Flutter to ensure smooth animations and cross-platform compatibility. It interacts with a lightweight local backend powered by FastAPI, which handles data processing via machine learning and generates responses using a SLM.
projectRefs: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?
